title: Chocolate mousse
summary: The bistro mousse made the old way: melted chocolate, egg yolks and beaten whites, nothing else to hide behind.
steps: Melt the chocolate and coconut oil together in a heatproof bowl set over barely simmering water, stirring until smooth. Take the bowl off the heat.
Whisk in the hot coffee and all but 2 tbsp of the powdered erythritol. The mixture will tighten, then loosen again as you keep whisking.

Let it cool for 5 minutes, then whisk in the yolks one at a time, followed by the vanilla, salt and stevia. Taste: unsweetened chocolate needs the sweetener adjusted to your liking now, before the whites go in.
In a clean bowl, whip the whites with the cream of tartar to soft peaks, then add the remaining 2 tbsp erythritol and whip to firm, glossy peaks.
Stir a quarter of the whites into the chocolate to lighten it, then fold in the rest in two additions with a large spatula, stopping as soon as no white streaks remain.
Spoon into six small glasses and refrigerate at least 4 hours, until set.
tips: The eggs are not cooked; use very fresh eggs, or pasteurised eggs if serving anyone vulnerable.
The chocolate must be warm but not hot when the yolks go in, or they will scramble; just warm to the lip is right.

origin.history: French cookery books of the 1700s already describe light, whipped chocolate preparations under the name mousse. The plain version of chocolate folded with beaten eggs became a fixture of French home and bistro cooking in the twentieth century, and from there spread worldwide.
